summary: Provides a pseudo Content Delivery Protocol that protects multiple source flows with one or more repair flows using the Forward Error Correction Framework and the SDP elements defined for it. It is not meant as a full protocol. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: If some pages of a book can be lost in the mail, you can send extra repair pages. This memo shows how one set of repair pages can cover several books.

questions: repair flows for forward error correction
how to protect multiple source flows with fec
subtitle: A blueprint for protecting multiple data flows with shared repair data.

tldr.problem: When delivering multiple data streams over networks, packet loss can corrupt any of them. Separate repair streams for each source are inefficient.
tldr.mechanism: This memo shows how to combine multiple source flows into source blocks, apply FEC (Forward Error Correction) to generate shared repair flows, and identify flows using Flow IDs in SDP descriptions.
tldr.outcome: Receivers can recover lost packets from any source flow using shared repair data, improving delivery efficiency for multicast and streaming applications.

today: RFC 6801 is published as Informational and has not been obsoleted. It serves as a practical guide for implementers using the FEC Framework to protect multiple flows.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 6801 explains how to use the Forward Error Correction (FEC) Framework and Session Description Protocol (SDP) elements to build a pseudo Content Delivery Protocol (CDP) for protecting multiple source flows with repair flows. Rather than defining a new protocol, it demonstrates how to combine existing standards to handle the practical case where one or more data streams need to be protected together.

The motivating use case is protecting multiple multicast flows—for example, video and audio streams—with a single repair stream. Traditional FEC typically protects one source independently; this memo shows how to multiplex multiple sources into shared source blocks.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo explains how to use the FEC standard pieces and network descriptions to protect several streaming channels with one backup channel.

sections.title: Multiplexing Flows into Source Blocks
sections.content:
The core idea is to collect packets from multiple source flows into a single source block. Each source flow is identified by a unique Flow ID (FID)—a short number defined in the SDP description—and associated with a tuple of IP addresses, ports, and protocol. At the sender, packets from all flows are bundled together, padding added if needed to match the FEC scheme's symbol size, and then passed to an FEC encoder.

The encoder generates repair symbols, which are grouped into repair payloads and sent out as a repair flow. Each repair payload carries a Repair FEC Payload ID that links it to a particular source block. Source payloads may also carry Explicit Source FEC Payload IDs to indicate their position if the flow cannot rely on implicit sequencing.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender takes pages from multiple books, groups them together, runs them through an error-protection program, and gets back both the original pages and extra repair pages labeled with which books they came from.

sections.title: Example: Two Source Flows and One Repair Flow
sections.content:
The RFC walks through a concrete example: protecting two multicast video flows (each to a different address, both on port 30000) with one repair flow. Each source flow is assigned a Flow ID (0 and 1). The SDP description binds each Flow ID to its source address and announces the repair flow's address. As packets arrive from each source, they are collected into source blocks of 10,000 bytes (Flow 1) and 7,000 bytes (Flow 2). Assuming a 512-byte symbol length and a 2/3 FEC code, the encoder generates 10 repair symbols for the first block and 7 for the second.

At the receiver, packets are mapped back to their Flow IDs using the SDP description, and the FEC decoder uses the Flow IDs and the Explicit Source FEC Payload IDs to reconstruct missing packets from the repair symbols.
sections.plainLanguage: Two streams arrive at different network addresses, each tagged with a flow number. The repair stream arrives at a third address. The receiver uses the flow numbers to figure out which packets are missing and reconstructs them.

sections.title: Reconstruction at the Receiver
sections.content:
When the receiver gets packets from the source flows and the repair flow, it first uses the SDP elements to map the network tuples to Flow IDs. The Repair FEC Payload ID tells the FEC decoder which source block the repair symbols protect. The Explicit Source FEC Payload IDs, combined with the known Flow ID ordering, let the decoder identify exactly which source symbols are missing and where.

The FEC scheme then performs decoding: if enough repair symbols have arrived to cover the losses, missing symbols are recovered. The decoder informs the CDP when symbols for each flow have been recovered, and after a timeout specified in the SDP (the repair window), any unrecovered packets are discarded and the next source block is processed.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver figures out which messages went missing and uses the repair symbols to figure out what they were, like solving a puzzle with the extra pieces.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: RFC 6801 is informational and does not add its own security requirements beyond those of the FEC Framework (RFC 6363) and the SDP elements (RFC 6364). The document notes that general network security considerations apply, such as authentication of the SDP description and integrity protection of the flow. Implementers should refer to the base framework documents for specifics.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo does not introduce new security issues; it just combines existing standards, so the same security precautions apply.
